title: ER-Reason: A Benchmark Dataset for LLM Clinical Reasoning in the Emergency Room
claim: A benchmark covers every stage of a real expert workflow, pairing each stage with its data source and the reasoning it requires.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right chain of five stages, dotted reasoning arcs above, data boxes below
description: A single wide diagram shows the emergency room workflow as five rounded yellow boxes connected by thick black arrows: Triage intake, EHR Review, Initial Assessment, Treatment choice and Disposition plan. Each box holds a black pictogram, such as a patient on a stretcher, a medical folder, a hospital bed, drugs and an IV bag, or a patient with an IV stand. Dotted curved arrows above the boxes carry labels for the clinician's reasoning, including pattern recognition, initial differential diagnosis formation, rule-out reasoning, decision factors, treatment planning, and the decision to admit, discharge or escalate. A blue 'Reasoning process' label with a doctor icon sits at top left. A yellow 'ER workflow' arrow and a pink 'ER-Reason benchmark data' label sit at left. Dashed grey boxes below each stage name the notes used, with a time axis of clinical-note icons under EHR Review.
caption: Overview of the ER-Reason benchmark. The benchmark dataset consists of de-identified, longitudinal clinical notes spanning a wide range of document types, including discharge summaries, progress notes, History and Physical exams, consult notes, imaging reports, and ER provider notes. The evaluation tasks cover all key stages of clinical decision-making in the ER workflow, including triage intake, initial assessment, treatment selection, disposition plan, and final diagnosis.
abstract: Existing benchmarks for evaluating the clinical reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) often lack a clear definition of "clinical reasoning" as a construct, fail to capture the full breadth of interdependent tasks within a clinical workflow, and rely on stylized vignettes rather than real-world clinical documentation. As a result, recent studies have found significant discrepancies between LLM performance on stylized benchmarks derived from medical licensing exams and their performance in real-world prospective studies. To address these limitations, we introduce ER-Reason, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLM reasoning as clinical evidence accumulates across decision-making tasks spanning the full workflow of emergency medicine. ER-Reason comprises 25,174 de-identified clinical notes from 3,437 patients, supporting evaluation across all stages of the emergency department workflow: triage intake, treatment selection, disposition planning, and final diagnosis. Crucially, evaluation in ER-Reason extends beyond diagnostic accuracy to include stepwise Script Concordance Test (SCT)-style questions grounded in real patient cases, which assess whether LLMs update their diagnostic beliefs in the correct direction and magnitude as clinical evidence accumulates, scored against 2,555 emergency physician annotations. We evaluate reasoning and non-reasoning LLMs on ER-Reason, and show that our tasks provide a more nuanced view of how LLM reasoning fails on real patient cases than existing benchmarks allow.
